# filters.linear { #wdm.filters.linear }

`filters.linear`

Linear Kalman filter, RTS smoother, and the local-linear-trend model.

Used in phase 1, where the only data available is a sequence of weights with no
food log. Nothing about metabolism can be estimated from that. What *can* be
estimated, and what phase 2 badly needs, is how noisy your scale readings are
and how fast your underlying trend genuinely moves.

The workhorse is the local linear trend model

$$
\begin{pmatrix} \mu_{k+1} \\ \beta_{k+1} \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \mu_k \\ \beta_k \end{pmatrix} + w_k,
\qquad y_k = \mu_k + v_k
$$

with $\mu$ the true weight level and $\beta$ its daily slope. It is
the simplest model that separates "the scale bounced" from "the trend moved",
which is precisely the separation phase 1 exists to quantify.

Note that this same filter, run on your data as it accumulates, is already the
single most useful thing here: the smoothed $\mu$ is a far better read on
where you actually are than any raw weigh-in, and $\beta$ is a direct
estimate of your current rate of loss with an honest error bar attached.

### kalman_filter { #wdm.filters.linear.kalman_filter }

```python
filters.linear.kalman_filter(y, observed, f, h, q, r, m0, p0, *, dof=None)
```

Forward pass of the linear-Gaussian Kalman filter.

Missing observations are handled by *skipping the update*, not by imputing a
value: the predicted belief is carried forward unchanged and contributes
nothing to the likelihood. This is the mathematically correct treatment of
missingness at random, and it is why gaps in your weigh-ins cost you
precision but never introduce bias.

#### Parameters {.doc-section .doc-section-parameters}

| Name     | Type                   | Description                                                                                                                                                  | Default    |
|----------|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|
| y        | Float\[Array, \' t\'\] | Observations, length ``t``. Entries where ``observed`` is zero are ignored and may be any finite value.                                                      | _required_ |
| observed | Float\[Array, \' t\'\] | 1.0 where an observation exists, 0.0 otherwise.                                                                                                              | _required_ |
| dof      | float \| None          | Degrees of freedom of Student-t observation noise, or ``None`` for the exact Gaussian Kalman filter. See `wdm.models.observation.student_t_inflation`. | `None`     |

### local_linear_trend_matrices { #wdm.filters.linear.local_linear_trend_matrices }

filters.linear.local_linear_trend_matrices()

### rts_smoother { #wdm.filters.linear.rts_smoother }

```python
filters.linear.rts_smoother(res, f)
```

Rauch-Tung-Striebel backward pass for a linear-Gaussian model.

Runs backwards from the final filtered belief, correcting each earlier
estimate with everything learned afterwards. The gain

$$
J_k = P_k F^\top (P_{k+1}^{-})^{-1}
$$

is solved rather than inverted, which matters when the predicted covariance
is poorly conditioned -- as it is on long stretches with no weigh-ins.

### trend_filter { #wdm.filters.linear.trend_filter }

```python
filters.linear.trend_filter(
    y,
    observed,
    level_sd,
    slope_sd,
    obs_sd,
    *,
    m0=None,
    p0=None,
    dof=None,
)
```

Local linear trend filter, parameterized by the three noise scales.

Gaussian observation noise unless ``dof`` selects Student-t; phase 1 and
phase 2 must use the same choice, so that the scale phase 1 identifies is
the scale phase 2 assumes.

The initial belief defaults to the first available observation with a wide
covariance -- a diffuse prior in all but name, which lets the data rather
than the guess determine the early trajectory.
